parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a field does to a tiny test charge placed in it - what quantity of force per what quantity of charge defines the strength?
parts.proper_answer: Electric field strength at a point is the force per unit positive charge acting on a stationary charge placed at that point.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Field Strength Means**
Imagine placing a very small positive test charge at a point in space. It feels a force $F$. The field strength $E$ tells you how much force each coulomb of charge would feel there, so $$E = \frac{F}{q}$$ where $q$ is positive. The word positive matters because direction of $E$ is defined as direction of force on a positive charge.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A potential difference of $2.5\text{ kV}$ is applied across a pair of horizontal metal plates in a vacuum, as shown in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1 (not to scale)

Each plate has a length of $5.9\text{ cm}$. The separation of the plates is $4.0\text{ cm}$. The arrangement produces a uniform electric field between the plates. Assume the field does not extend beyond the edges of the plates.

An electron enters the field at point A with horizontal velocity $3.7 \times 10^7\text{ m s}^{-1}$ along a line mid-way between the plates. The electron leaves the field at point B.
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the electron to move from A to B.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the horizontal direction from A to B - there is no horizontal force, so think about how horizontal distance, horizontal speed and time are linked.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate Horizontal From Vertical**
Between the plates the electric force is vertical only, so horizontally the electron just coasts at constant $v_x = 3.7 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. The horizontal distance to cover is the plate length $L = 5.9 \text{ cm} = 5.9 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Time From Constant Speed**
For uniform motion $$t = \frac{L}{v_x} = \frac{5.9 \times 10^{-2}}{3.7 \times 10^7} = 1.6 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s}$$ This is the time spent in the field, and it will control how long the vertical force has to act.

hints: Hint 1: Focus on the horizontal direction from A to B - there is no horizontal force, so think about how horizontal distance, horizontal speed and time are linked.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength.
hints: Hint 1: Look at what creates the uniform field between the plates - a voltage across a separation - and recall how field strength relates to those two quantities.
Hint 2: Check your units before dividing - the separation must be in metres, not centimetres, and the voltage in volts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Uniform Field Formula**
For parallel plates the field is uniform and $$E = \frac{V}{d}$$ where $V$ is the p.d. across the plates and $d$ is their separation.

Step 2: **Put Numbers In SI Units**
Here $V = 2.5 \text{ kV} = 2500 \text{ V}$ and $d = 4.0 \text{ cm} = 4.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$. So $$E = \frac{2500}{4.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 6.25 \times 10^{4} \text{ N C}^{-1} \approx 6.3 \times 10^{4} \text{ N C}^{-1}$$ directed from the positive upper plate to the negative lower plate.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Show that the acceleration of the electron in the field is $1.1 \times 10^{16}\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
hints: Hint 1: Start from the two ways of writing the vertical force on the electron - one from the field acting on its charge, and one from its mass times acceleration.
Hint 2: Remember the standard values for the electron charge magnitude and mass, and combine the two force expressions to isolate acceleration.
parts.proper_answer: $a = Eq/m = 1.1 \times 10^{16} \text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards towards positive plate.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Field To Acceleration**
The electric force magnitude is $$F = Eq$$ and Newton's second law gives $$F = ma$$ So $$a = \frac{Eq}{m}$$

Step 2: **Calculate The Value**
Use $E = 6.25 \times 10^{4} \text{ N C}^{-1}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$: $$a = \frac{(6.25 \times 10^{4})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{16} \text{ m s}^{-2}$$ The electron is negative so the force and acceleration are upwards towards the positive upper plate.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Use the acceleration given in **(iii)** and your answer in **(i)** to determine the vertical distance $y$ between point B and the upper plate.

markscheme_points.text: distance from plate $= 2.0 - 1.4$ $= 0.6 \text{cm}$ (allow 1 or more s.f.)

hints: Hint 1: Think about the vertical motion starting at A - what is the initial vertical velocity, and which kinematic equation links vertical displacement to acceleration and the time in the field?
Hint 2: Calculate the upward shift of the electron from the central line, remembering to square the very small time from (i).
Hint 3: Look at Fig. 2.1 to see how that upward shift relates to the required gap y - the electron starts 2.0 cm below the top plate.
parts.proper_answer: Vertical deflection $= 1.4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 1.4 \text{ cm}$, so $y = 2.0 - 1.4 = 0.60 \text{ cm}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Vertical Motion Starts From Rest**
Vertically the electron enters with $u_y = 0$ and accelerates upwards at $a = 1.1 \times 10^{16} \text{ m s}^{-2}$ for time $t = 1.6 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s}$. Displacement is $$s_y = u_y t + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = \frac{1}{2}at^2$$

Step 2: **Find The Upward Deflection**
$$s_y = \frac{1}{2} \times (1.1 \times 10^{16}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-9})^2 \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 1.4 \text{ cm}$$ This is how far it has risen above the mid-line by point B.

Step 3: **Convert To Gap y**
At A the gap to the upper plate is $2.0 \text{ cm}$. After rising $1.4 \text{ cm}$ the remaining gap is $$y = 2.0 - 1.4 = 0.6 \text{ cm}$$ So the electron leaves much closer to the top plate but does not hit it.

parts.label: (b)(v)
parts.text: Explain why the calculation in **(iv)** does not need to include the gravitational effects on the electron.

markscheme_points.text: electric force >> gravitational force (on electron)/weight or acceleration due to electric field >> acceleration due to gravitational field

hints: Hint 1: Compare orders of magnitude - think how huge the electric acceleration $10^{16} \text{ m s}^{-2}$ is next to the gravitational acceleration $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
parts.proper_answer: The electric force on the electron is very much greater than its weight, so gravitational effects are negligible.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Gravity Can Be Ignored**
Electric acceleration is about $10^{16} \text{ m s}^{-2}$ while gravitational acceleration is only $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. Equivalently $Eq >> mg$. Gravity would add a deflection about $10^{15}$ times smaller, completely negligible over $10^{-9} \text{ s}$.

parts.label: (b)(vi)
parts.text:
The electron enters the field at time $t = 0$.

On Fig. 2.2, sketch graphs to show the variation with time $t$ of

1. the horizontal component $v_{X}$ of the velocity of the electron,

2. the vertical component $v_{Y}$ of the velocity of the electron.

Numerical values are not required.

{{figure:figure_2_2}}

Fig. 2.2

markscheme_points.text: $v_{x}$–$t$ graph: horizontal line at a non-zero value of $v_{x}$
$v_{y}$–$t$ graph: straight line through the origin with positive gradient

hints: Hint 1: Think separately about forces in each direction - with no horizontal force, what does that imply for how $v_x$ changes with time?
Hint 2: Vertically there is a constant force from the uniform field, so think about what kind of motion that produces starting from zero vertical speed.
parts.proper_answer: $v_x$-$t$: horizontal straight line at non-zero $v_x$. $v_y$-$t$: straight line through origin with positive constant gradient.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Horizontal Component $v_x$**
No horizontal force means no horizontal acceleration, so $v_x$ stays constant at $3.7 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. On a $v_x$ against $t$ graph this is a horizontal line above the time axis, starting at a non-zero intercept at $t = 0$.

Step 2: **Vertical Component $v_y$**
Vertically there is a constant electric force and hence constant acceleration $a$. Starting with $v_y = 0$ at $t = 0$, velocity grows linearly: $v_y = at$. On a $v_y$ against $t$ graph this is a straight line through the origin with positive constant gradient.
